 Opinion | Do we really need another national awareness month? 
 Phoebe Baldasare | Staff Reporter 
 Nov 18, 2026 
 1 hr ago 
 Comments

 It's November, which means it's National Gratitude Month. Except it's not. Despite Thanksgiving being one of the 12 recognized federal holidays , National Gratitude Month technically doesn't exist. Neither do Historic Bridge Awareness Month, Gluten-Free Diet Awareness Month, National Peanut Butter Lovers Month, National Sweet Potato Awareness Month or any of the other national months for November that pop up online. 
 These awareness months are largely unofficial, created by individuals and organizations to celebrate causes, interests or products they feel passionate about, no matter how unusual they may seem. But the reason these months continue to emerge is not quite as simple as personal passion. There's a larger connection at play: the economy. 
 National months are a useful promotional tool, alongside national holidays and weeks. Essentially, these observances provide free marketing. People pick them up on social media, purchase products and share their experiences online. One of the biggest examples is National Girlfriends Day . 
 Every Aug. 1, Instagram fills with stories of women receiving flowers and gifts from their partners. On the surface, it looks like Valentine's Day 2.0. However, National Girlfriends Day wasn't originally about romance. Its intended purpose was to give female friends an opportunity to get together and celebrate their friendships. Over time, the holiday has taken on a more commercial meaning, creating another opportunity to sell traditional Valentine's Day gifts just six months after the holiday. 
 Holidays have long been used as opportunities to sell products. Thanksgiving sells turkeys, Halloween sells costumes and Christmas sells gifts. Each holiday has its own industry, with stores filling their shelves with decorations and themed products to encourage customers to spend more each year. It makes sense why corporations want to capitalize on holidays when consumers are already looking to make purchases. 
 As a consumer, what's more appealing: buying raisin bread simply because you see it on a grocery store shelf or buying it because it's National Raisin Bread Month? Would you rather visit an ice cream parlor on an ordinary day or celebrate National Ice Cream Month? 
 When it comes to federally recognized observance months, there are two primary categories: national health observances and national heritage and history months. There are exceptions, as Congress can also designate temporary observances for specific causes or events. 
 For the most part, however, actually recognized observance months stick to this. For example, Pride Month, Black History Month, Immigrant Heritage Month and more are all history and heritage months recognized by the United States government. There are many more National Health Observances , like Heart Health Month, Breast Cancer Awareness Month and more. 
 The reason these monthly observances were created was to bring awareness to these causes, whether it was to celebrate cultural heritage, remember history or promote safety throughout the U.S. They are more than just an excuse to have fun, but a vital part in creating a safer and healthier human experience. 
 Therefore, when people buy into all of these corporate holidays, it reduces the value of existing awareness months. It creates an oversaturation of awareness when there are 20 different awareness months packed into one month. National Diabetes Month and National Banana Pudding Lovers Month are both in November, and only the first one serves the purpose of an awareness month. 
 Thus, as a society, we need to stop creating more and more pointless awareness months and holidays. They are just a marketing solution that has forced actual issues into the background. 
 Celebrating these holidays isn't a bad thing. These months and holidays can create joy within individuals while turning passion into communities. Just remember that when you are celebrating National Candle Month , you are buying into more than just candles – you are supporting a system that is making society buy more things while we forget the reason we started celebrating to begin with.
